title: Fragments
scopeHtml: Fragment lifecycle vs view lifecycle, FragmentManager hierarchy, transactions and back stack, Fragment Result API, ViewModel scoping, FragmentFactory, DialogFragment, ViewPager2, state restoration, and Fragment-specific production failures. (Process death mechanics are owned by the process-death chunk; Navigation internals by A4; here only fragment-hosting behaviour.)

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the Fragment lifecycle. Why does a Fragment have both a lifecycle and a "view lifecycle", and in which callback would you do what?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most Fragment bugs (leaks, duplicate observers, crashes after navigation) come from not knowing that the Fragment instance outlives its view.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A Fragment goes onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onViewStateRestored, onStart, onResume, then back down through onPause, onStop, onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach. The key point is that the Fragment instance and its view have separate lifetimes. When a fragment goes on the back stack, onDestroyView runs but the instance survives in CREATED state, and onCreateView runs again on return. So anything that touches views belongs to the view lifecycle, available through viewLifecycleOwner, and anything that is instance-level, like arguments and non-view setup, belongs in onCreate."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Fragment is a UI controller managed by a FragmentManager. The manager drives each fragment through states, and the host's state caps what a fragment can reach (a fragment cannot be RESUMED if its Activity is only STARTED).

Fragment instance:  onAttach -> onCreate ----------------------------------- onDestroy -> onDetach
View (may repeat):                 onCreateView -> onViewCreated -> onViewStateRestored
                                      -> onStart -> onResume -> onPause -> onStop -> onDestroyView
Fragment Lifecycle states:  INITIALIZED -> CREATED -> STARTED -> RESUMED
View Lifecycle (viewLifecycleOwner):  INITIALIZED -> CREATED -> STARTED -> RESUMED -> DESTROYED

Two Lifecycle objects exist:

  • fragment.lifecycle follows the instance. It reaches DESTROYED only at onDestroy.
  • fragment.viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle is created with onCreateView and reaches DESTROYED at onDestroyView. It is a new one each time the view is created. Reading viewLifecycleOwner when view == null (before onCreateView returns, after onDestroyView, or if the fragment returns no view) throws IllegalStateException: Can't access the Fragment View's LifecycleOwner when getView() is null.

Where to put what:

Callback Use
onAttach Rarely needed; host/context available
onCreate Read arguments, restore non-view state, init non-view objects. No views yet
onCreateView Inflate and return root only (or use Fragment(R.layout.x) constructor)
onViewCreated Find/bind views, set adapters and listeners, observe state with viewLifecycleOwner
onViewStateRestored View state (EditText content, scroll) has been restored; rarely used
onStart/onResume Same semantics as Activity: visible / interactive
onDestroyView Null out view references (binding, adapters), release view-bound resources
onDestroy Instance is going away (not guaranteed to run on process death)

onViewStateRestored runs after onViewCreated and before onStart. A Fragment that is replaced and put on the back stack goes onPause, onStop, onDestroyView and stays CREATED; popping it reruns onCreateView, onViewCreated, onViewStateRestored, onStart, onResume.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    private val vm: ProfileViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val userId = requireArguments().getString("userId") // instance-level, safe here
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        // View-level: observers are bound to the VIEW lifecycle
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                vm.state.collect { render(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using this (the Fragment) as LifecycleOwner for view-related observers; they stack up on every onViewCreated.
  • Treating onDestroy as the place to clean up views; views die at onDestroyView.
  • Assuming onCreateView runs once; it runs every time the fragment returns from the back stack.
  • Touching viewLifecycleOwner in onCreate or after onDestroyView.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is the Fragment's own lifecycle DESTROYED but its view's is not? → Never; the view lifecycle ends first (onDestroyView precedes onDestroy).
  2. What state is a fragment in on the back stack? → CREATED; instance and ViewModel alive, view destroyed.
  3. What does a fragment that returns null from onCreateView have? → No view lifecycle; viewLifecycleOwner throws, and view-related callbacks do not run.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites the callback list. The senior frames it as "instance lifetime vs view lifetime", states where each kind of resource must be bound and released, and knows the failure modes (duplicate observers, leaked bindings, IllegalStateException on viewLifecycleOwner).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "toast shown twice after back navigation" bug that took a team a day: observers were registered with this in onViewCreated, so each return from the back stack added another observer.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between supportFragmentManager, parentFragmentManager and childFragmentManager, and when would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Picking the wrong manager is a classic cause of "fragment not found", wrong back stack, and lost results.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each FragmentActivity has one FragmentManager, supportFragmentManager. Each Fragment has two references: parentFragmentManager, the manager that holds this fragment (the activity's or a parent fragment's), and childFragmentManager, its own manager for fragments nested inside it. Siblings talk through the parent manager; nesting uses the child one. getFragmentManager() is deprecated in favour of parentFragmentManager."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fragments form a tree. Each node that can host fragments owns a FragmentManager, and each manager has its own transaction queue and back stack.

Activity (supportFragmentManager)
 ├─ HostFragment A   (A.parentFragmentManager == activity.supportFragmentManager)
 │    └─ ChildFragment (child.parentFragmentManager == A.childFragmentManager)
 └─ Fragment B       (sibling of A, same manager)
  • A child fragment's lifecycle is capped by its parent's. When the parent fragment is stopped or its view destroyed, children follow.
  • Back stack entries pushed on childFragmentManager are separate from the activity's. Pressing back pops the innermost handled entry first when the child's transaction was setPrimaryNavigationFragment-ed (the primary navigation fragment gets back priority) or a callback is registered; otherwise the activity-level stack wins. Cross-check this against your back handling.
  • Fragment Result API keys are per FragmentManager: sender and listener must use the same manager (siblings: parentFragmentManager; parent listening to child: parent registers on childFragmentManager, child sends via parentFragmentManager).
  • parentFragmentManager throws IllegalStateException: Fragment X not associated with a fragment manager if the fragment is not currently added (e.g. called after detach in an async callback).
  • Rule for nesting UI inside a fragment: use childFragmentManager and a FragmentContainerView inside the parent's layout, never requireActivity().supportFragmentManager with a container that lives in the parent's view (the child would outlive the parent's view and crash or leak).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Parent hosting a nested fragment
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    if (savedInstanceState == null) { // manager restores children itself
        childFragmentManager.commit {
            setReorderingAllowed(true)
            replace(R.id.child_container, DetailFragment())
        }
    }
}

// Broken: container belongs to the parent's view, but we use the Activity's manager
requireActivity().supportFragmentManager.commit { replace(R.id.child_container, DetailFragment()) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using activity.supportFragmentManager for nested containers; after the parent's view is destroyed, the child's view container is gone.
  • Sending a fragment result on childFragmentManager and listening on parentFragmentManager (different channels).
  • Adding the child on every onViewCreated without a savedInstanceState == null guard, producing duplicates (see the duplicate-fragment scenario).
  • Calling childFragmentManager before the fragment is attached.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a child fragment outlive its parent? → No; child states are capped by the parent's state.
  2. Which FragmentManager does getFragmentManager() return? → The same as parentFragmentManager, but nullable and deprecated.
  3. How does back press reach a nested fragment's back stack? → Via the primary navigation fragment chain / OnBackPressedCallbacks; the child manager's back stack pops only if it holds the primary navigation fragment's chain or a callback is registered (verify behaviour against your Fragment version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "child is for nested fragments". Senior: describes the tree, state capping, per-manager back stacks and result keys, and the container-ownership rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Tab screens whose nested fragments were added via the Activity's manager crashed with "No view found for id" after rotation, because the parent view was recreated after the child was restored.

questions.promptHtml: In a Fragment, when do you pass viewLifecycleOwner instead of this to observe(), collect and similar APIs? What goes wrong with this?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the single most common Fragment lifecycle bug, and it tests whether you understand that observers outlive the view.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Anything that updates views must be bound to viewLifecycleOwner. The Fragment's own lifecycle keeps running while the fragment sits on the back stack with no view. If I observe LiveData with this in onViewCreated, the observer is not removed when the view dies, and each return adds another one, so I get duplicate updates, work against a destroyed view, and leaked views. With viewLifecycleOwner the observer dies with the view."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LiveData removes an observer when its owner reaches DESTROYED. The fragment's lifecycle reaches DESTROYED only at onDestroy. On the back stack, the fragment stays CREATED for minutes or hours.

Fragment A shown:   onViewCreated #1  -> observe(this) #1
navigate to B:      onDestroyView (A.lifecycle still CREATED -> observer #1 still alive)
back to A:          onViewCreated #2  -> observe(this) #2   // now two observers
LiveData emits:     both run; #1 captured the old binding -> touches destroyed views

Rules:

  • View/UI collection: viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope + repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) (lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4+) or flowWithLifecycle. lifecycleScope of the Fragment itself is cancelled only at onDestroy, so collecting a Flow in lifecycleScope.launch from onViewCreated has the same leak/duplication problem.
  • Non-UI, fragment-instance work (e.g. registering registerForActivityResult, setting FragmentResultListener on the fragment manager with the fragment as owner when the result handling should survive view recreation) may use this.
  • launchWhenStarted and friends are deprecated; they pause rather than cancel the upstream flow. Prefer repeatOnLifecycle.
  • Android Lint has a check (FragmentLiveDataObserve) that warns about observe(this) in onCreateView/onViewCreated/onActivityCreated (verify the exact id in your lint version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
    vm.items.observe(this) { adapter.submitList(it) }          // stacks on each recreate
    lifecycleScope.launch { vm.events.collect { show(it) } }   // runs until onDestroy, even viewless
}

// Correct
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
    vm.items.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { adapter.submitList(it) }
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            vm.events.collect { show(it) }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing LiveData "handles lifecycle for you" regardless of which owner you pass.
  • Using lifecycleScope inside onViewCreated for collecting UI state.
  • Using viewLifecycleOwner inside onCreate or from a DialogFragment that overrides only onCreateDialog (no view lifecycle, so it throws).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a fragment on the back stack still receive LiveData updates? → Observers bound to this do; those bound to viewLifecycleOwner are removed.
  2. Difference between launchWhenStarted and repeatOnLifecycle? → The first suspends the coroutine when stopped but keeps upstream producers active; the second cancels and restarts the block.
  3. Why can observing in onCreate with viewLifecycleOwner never work? → The view lifecycle is created after onCreateView, so the owner is not available yet.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use viewLifecycleOwner to avoid leaks". Senior explains the back-stack scenario, covers Flow and coroutine scopes (not only LiveData), and mentions the lint check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dashboard showed duplicated snackbars after tab switching, traced to observe(this) in onViewCreated of a fragment that was replaced/popped repeatedly.

questions.promptHtml: Why does holding a ViewBinding reference in a Fragment leak, and what is the correct pattern?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Leaking the view tree is the standard memory bug in fragment code; LeakCanary flags it constantly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A Fragment instance can outlive its view, for example on the back stack. If the Fragment holds a binding field, it keeps the whole view tree alive, which holds the Activity context, bitmaps and adapters, after onDestroyView. The fix is to null the binding in onDestroyView, usually with a nullable backing field _binding and a non-null binding getter, and to clear things like RecyclerView adapters and ViewPager2 adapters too."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reference chain: Fragment (back stack) -> binding -> root view -> Context (Activity) -> everything. The view hierarchy is conceptually garbage after onDestroyView, but the Fragment's field keeps it reachable. With a 3 MB view tree (images + RecyclerView with cached ViewHolders) and a back stack of 5 such fragments, that is roughly 15 MB retained for no benefit; with a leaked Activity (the views hold it) it becomes the whole Activity graph after a rotation, since the retained fragment on the back stack is recreated with the new Activity while the old view still points to the old Activity.

Standard pattern:

  • private var _binding: FragmentFooBinding? = null; private val binding get() = _binding!!
  • Assign in onCreateView (or onViewCreated with FragmentFooBinding.bind(view) when using the layout constructor), null in onDestroyView.
  • Other view-scoped fields (adapters referencing views, ViewPager2.adapter, RecyclerView.adapter, listeners to singleton objects, ValueAnimators, MapView / WebView) need explicit cleanup.
  • LeakCanary message to recognise: "Fragment received Fragment#onDestroyView() callback (references to its views should be cleared to prevent leaks)" (leak-report text, paraphrased).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_feed) {
    private var _binding: FragmentFeedBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!   // only valid between onViewCreated and onDestroyView

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentFeedBinding.bind(view)
        binding.list.adapter = FeedAdapter()
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        binding.list.adapter = null // adapter holds ViewHolders -> views
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• lateinit var binding that is never cleared.
  • Accessing binding from a coroutine that continues after onDestroyView (NPE via _binding!!); tie such work to viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Nulling _binding but leaving private val adapter = FeedAdapter(binding) created in onCreate.
  • Using the pattern in an Activity (unnecessary).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does an Activity need this? → No; the Activity's views die with it.
  2. Why not by lazy for binding? → It is bound to a specific view instance; lazy keeps the first one forever.
  3. How would you remove the boilerplate safely? → A viewBinding property delegate that registers a DefaultLifecycleObserver on viewLifecycleOwner and clears its reference on ON_DESTROY; post the clearing so it runs after your own onDestroyView code (the viewLifecycleOwner DESTROYED event fires before onDestroyView() returns, so the delegate usually posts the nulling).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "null it in onDestroyView". Senior explains the reachability chain, quantifies it, covers adapters and async work after the view is gone, and knows the delegate-timing subtlety.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-heavy app saw OOM rates rise on low-end phones after a back-stack-based flow went live; heap dumps showed destroyed fragment views retained through binding fields.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between commit(), commitNow(), commitAllowingStateLoss() and commitNowAllowingStateLoss()? Why do we see "Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common Fragment crash in production dashboards, and the "just use AllowingStateLoss" answer separates levels.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "commit() schedules the transaction asynchronously on the main thread; commitNow() runs it synchronously but cannot be added to the back stack. Both throw IllegalStateException if the FragmentManager has already saved its state, because a change after saving would be lost when the process is killed and the UI restored. AllowingStateLoss variants skip the check and accept that the change may be lost. The proper fix is not to suppress the exception but to avoid issuing transactions when state is saved, by tying the trigger to the lifecycle, or to accept loss only for transient UI."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State saving: FragmentActivity.onSaveInstanceState calls the manager's saveAllState() and marks the manager as stateSaved. From then until the Activity starts again, any new transaction would not be in the saved Bundle. If the system restores from that Bundle after process death, the UI would differ from what the user last saw, so the framework throws.

Timing by OS: on API 28+ onSaveInstanceState runs after onStop; on older versions between onPause and onStop. Do not hard-code this; use fragmentManager.isStateSaved.

Method Sync? Back stack? State loss check
commit() async (posted to main thread) yes throws if saved
commitNow() sync no (throws if addToBackStack) throws if saved
commitAllowingStateLoss() async yes no check
commitNowAllowingStateLoss() sync no no check

Also: executePendingTransactions() forces pending async commits; it is not allowed re-entrantly (calling it inside a transaction callback throws "FragmentManager is already executing transactions").

Typical triggers: network callback arrives after the user backgrounded the app; onActivityResult (delivered before onResume, after state was saved) in older code; FCM/event bus handlers; coroutine launched in lifecycleScope that resumes later.

Fixes in order of preference:

  1. Do UI-navigation work only when the lifecycle is at least STARTED: collect events inside repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED); events arriving while stopped wait in a Channel/SharedFlow with replay or in state (pendingNavigation).
  2. Guard with if (!parentFragmentManager.isStateSaved); else defer.
  3. Model the target screen as state, not an event ("current screen = X"), so applying it on return is naturally safe.
  4. commitAllowingStateLoss only where losing the change is harmless (a transient banner/loading overlay), and note that it must be a conscious decision.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Crashes if the response arrives after onSaveInstanceState
api.load().enqueue { supportFragmentManager.commit { replace(R.id.container, ResultFragment()) } }

// Safer: state-driven, applied only while STARTED
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.screen.collect { screen ->
            if (!supportFragmentManager.isStateSaved) {
                supportFragmentManager.commit {
                    setReorderingAllowed(true)
                    replace(R.id.container, screen.toFragment())
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blanket commitAllowingStateLoss() which can restore a stale UI after process death (e.g. user sees a screen from before the transaction).
  • Believing commitNow() avoids the check (it does not).
  • Using commitNow() together with addToBackStack (throws).
  • Calling executePendingTransactions() from inside lifecycle callbacks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the check there if the user would never see state loss? → Only the process-death restore path reveals it; the check protects UI consistency in that rare path.
  2. Does the Navigation component avoid this? → NavController also drives transactions and can hit the same exception if you call navigate() while state is saved; same remedy (navigate from STARTED-scoped collectors).
  3. How do you test this? → Background the app with "Don't keep activities" or adb shell am kill flows, trigger the callback in the background via a delayed task/IdlingResource, and assert no crash.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use commitAllowingStateLoss". Senior explains why the check exists, which methods are sync, and moves the design to lifecycle-scoped, state-driven navigation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow crashed for about 0.4% of sessions: the payment callback came back while the user had switched to a banking app, and the callback did a replace(); the fix was to keep the result as state and render it on STARTED.

questions.subtopic: add vs replace and back stack
questions.promptHtml: What does replace() vs add() do to existing fragments, and what exactly does addToBackStack() change in lifecycle terms? What happens to the replaced fragment's view and instance?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People assume "back stack = fragment kept alive with its view", which is wrong and causes state-loss and leak bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "add() puts a fragment next to existing ones in the container; replace() removes every fragment currently in that container and adds the new one. Without addToBackStack, the removed fragment is destroyed completely (onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach). With addToBackStack, the transaction is reversible: the removed fragment keeps its instance in CREATED state but its view is destroyed, so on pop it gets onCreateView again with restored view state. For add(), the old fragment's view stays alive but gets covered, which means it still receives touches if the new view is not opaque or clickable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• replace(containerId, f) is remove for all fragments in the container plus add(f).
  • Back stack records transactions, not fragments. Popping reverses the operations.
  • State comparison on replace + addToBackStack: old fragment -> onPause, onStop, onDestroyView (instance remains CREATED). Pop: onCreateView, onViewCreated, onViewStateRestored, onStart, onResume.
  • Without back stack: also onDestroy, onDetach; a ViewModel scoped to that fragment is cleared (onCleared).
  • add() + hide()/show(): view stays, no lifecycle callbacks are driven; only onHiddenChanged. Avoid for large graphs; memory is pinned and lifecycle (RESUMED) stays on hidden fragments unless you use setMaxLifecycle(f, STARTED).
  • View state: EditText/CheckBox etc. with an id are saved in onDestroyView time into the fragment's view-state SparseArray and restored in onViewStateRestored. Custom state or RecyclerView position is yours to restore (scroll state via layout manager is restored by RecyclerView only if the adapter is attached and stateRestorationPolicy allows).
  • setReorderingAllowed(true) lets the manager optimize overlapping operations in one transaction; Navigation and the Fragment KTX docs assume it. It is required for some features (shared element transitions, setMaxLifecycle ordering).
  • Pop options: popBackStack() (async), popBackStackImmediate() (sync), popBackStack(name, flags); POP_BACK_STACK_INCLUSIVE.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
supportFragmentManager.commit {
    setReorderingAllowed(true)
    replace(R.id.container, DetailFragment.newInstance(id), "detail")
    addToBackStack("detail")   // reversible
}

// Pop everything above (and including) "list"
supportFragmentManager.popBackStack("list", FragmentManager.POP_BACK_STACK_INCLUSIVE)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using add() over an existing fragment without making the covered view non-interactive (taps pass through to the lower one).
  • Assuming fields set in onCreateView survive; only the instance fields and ViewModel do.
  • Expecting onDestroy when the fragment goes onto the back stack.
  • Forgetting that replace into a container that contained several fragments removes all of them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the fragment's ViewModel cleared when replaced onto the back stack? → No; only when the fragment is finally destroyed (popped off or removed without back stack).
  2. Why setReorderingAllowed(true)? → Allows operation reordering/optimization and is needed for correct state changes with transitions; without it, intermediate fragments may be briefly created.
  3. How do you keep a heavy fragment alive for tab switching? → Prefer ViewPager2 or Navigation with state saving; hide/show costs memory and misleads lifecycle, so use setMaxLifecycle if you do it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "back stack lets you go back". Senior states what is destroyed at each step, ViewModel lifetime, the touch-through issue with add(), and when view state is saved/restored.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A form fragment lost RecyclerView scroll and typed text after back navigation because the field's EditText had no id (view state not saved), and the data was not in the ViewModel.

questions.promptHtml: How do two fragments (or a DialogFragment and its host) exchange results today? Why was setTargetFragment / onActivityResult replaced, and what are the delivery semantics of the Fragment Result API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks modern Fragment practice and understanding of lifecycle-aware delivery, including the "result delivered twice" trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use the Fragment Result API: the receiver calls setFragmentResultListener(requestKey, viewLifecycleOwner) on the FragmentManager both fragments share, and the sender calls setFragmentResult(requestKey, bundle). Delivery is lifecycle-aware: if the receiver is not at least STARTED, the result is held and delivered when it is. Only the latest result per key is kept. It survives process death because the results are saved with the manager. It replaces setTargetFragment, which created hidden coupling and was deprecated."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The FragmentManager holds a map requestKey -> Bundle (results) and requestKey -> listener. Internally:

  • setFragmentResult(key, bundle): if a listener is registered and its lifecycle is at least STARTED, deliver immediately; otherwise store the bundle (overwrites a previous one for the same key).
  • setFragmentResultListener(key, lifecycleOwner, listener): registers a lifecycle observer; on ON_START, if a stored result exists, it is delivered and cleared. When the owner is DESTROYED, the listener is removed. You can also call clearFragmentResult(key) / clearFragmentResultListener(key).
  • The stored results are part of FragmentManagerState, so a pending result survives rotation and process death (the Bundle must be parcelable and small).

Managers must match:

Sender Receiver registers on Sender uses
Sibling or DialogFragment shown from fragment F F.parentFragmentManager parentFragmentManager
Parent receives from child parent's childFragmentManager child's parentFragmentManager (which is the parent's child manager)
Fragment (hosted by Activity) receives from Activity parentFragmentManager (== supportFragmentManager) supportFragmentManager

Pitfalls: results are not for long-lived or high-frequency communication (use a shared ViewModel), and do not cross different Activities (use Activity Result API).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Receiver
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
    parentFragmentManager.setFragmentResultListener(
        "color_picker", viewLifecycleOwner
    ) { _, bundle -> apply(bundle.getInt("color")) }
}

// Sender (e.g. inside a DialogFragment)
parentFragmentManager.setFragmentResult("color_picker", bundleOf("color" to selected))
dismiss()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Registering the listener with the fragment (this) in onViewCreated, so it re-registers each view creation and can re-run stale delivery; use viewLifecycleOwner for UI results.
  • Using different keys or managers on the two sides, so nothing arrives and nothing throws.
  • Assuming multiple results queue up; the latest overwrites.
  • Putting a large object into the Bundle (counts against the saved-state transaction budget).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the receiver is on the back stack when the result is sent? → It is stored and delivered when the receiver reaches STARTED again.
  2. When would you pick a shared ViewModel instead? → Continuous or frequent state, more than a small Bundle, or complex objects.
  3. Why was setTargetFragment problematic? → Hidden dependency on instance identity, fragile after recreation, and lifecycle-unaware.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the API. Senior knows the lifecycle semantics, the manager-matching rule, persistence across process death and when not to use it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A date-picker dialog result was silently lost because the dialog used activity.supportFragmentManager while the listener was on parentFragmentManager of a nested fragment.

questions.promptHtml: How do fragments share a ViewModel, and how do you choose the scope: fragment, parent fragment, Activity, or navigation graph? What are the lifetime and staleness consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Scoping is where architecture meets lifecycle; wrong scope means either stale data or lost state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A ViewModel lives as long as its ViewModelStoreOwner. by viewModels() scopes to the fragment, by viewModels({ requireParentFragment() }) to the parent, by activityViewModels() to the Activity, and by navGraphViewModels(R.id.graph) to a Navigation graph back stack entry. I pick the smallest scope that covers every consumer. Activity scope is easy but long-lived and global to the screen, which leads to stale data when a flow is re-entered and hidden coupling between unrelated screens. A nav-graph scope matches a flow like checkout and is cleared when the flow is popped."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ViewModelProvider(owner) looks up a ViewModelStore held by the owner; the store survives configuration changes via NonConfigurationInstances (Activity) and is cleared when the owner is finished/destroyed for good. For fragments, the store lives in FragmentManagerViewModel of the parent manager, kept across recreation and cleared when the fragment is removed permanently (not when it is merely on the back stack).

Scope Owner Cleared when
viewModels() this fragment fragment removed permanently
viewModels(ownerProducer = { requireParentFragment() }) parent fragment parent removed
activityViewModels() host activity activity finishes (not rotation)
navGraphViewModels(graphId) NavBackStackEntry of the graph that graph is popped
hiltViewModel() nearest NavBackStackEntry / owner same as owner

Consequences:

  • Activity scope: the VM outlives the fragments. A second visit to the same screen sees old state unless reset explicitly (stale search text, old selected item, an old error state).
  • Two fragments in the same Activity that both use activityViewModels<X>() share one instance; two unrelated features using the same class unintentionally share too.
  • by viewModels() called with the wrong owner (e.g. in a child fragment expecting the parent's data) yields a separate instance and "data is null" bugs.
  • ViewModel must not hold View, Fragment, or Activity references (leak: it outlives them).
  • Constructor args need a ViewModelProvider.Factory or SavedStateHandle; by default, only SavedStateHandle-aware AbstractSavedStateViewModelFactory/CreationExtras (lifecycle 2.5+) is injected automatically.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ListFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_list) {
    private val shared: SelectionViewModel by activityViewModels()  // Activity scope
}

class StepTwoFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_step2) {
    // Scoped to the checkout nav graph: cleared when the whole flow is popped
    private val checkout: CheckoutViewModel by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph)
}

class ChildFragment : Fragment() {
    private val parentVm: ParentViewModel by viewModels(ownerProducer = { requireParentFragment() })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using activityViewModels for everything "to share easily".
  • Forgetting that navGraphViewModels requires the graph to be on the back stack when requested (crashes with IllegalArgumentException: No destination with ID ... is on the NavController's back stack).
  • Storing selection as a one-shot event in an Activity-scoped VM, which re-delivers on later visits.
  • Assuming the VM survives process death; it does not (see saved state / SavedStateHandle in the process-death chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a Fragment ViewModel survive going to the back stack? → Yes; it is cleared only when the fragment is permanently removed.
  2. How do you reset an Activity-scoped VM on re-entry? → Explicit reset() on entry/exit or move to a narrower scope such as a nav graph.
  3. How would two siblings in a ViewPager2 share a VM with their host fragment? → Scope to the host (parent) via requireParentFragment().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "activityViewModels to share data". Senior picks scope by flow lifetime, anticipates staleness and leak risks, and has a reset story.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen reopened with the previous query and results because an Activity-scoped VM was shared by "Search" in two navigation entry points.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Fragments require a no-arg constructor, how does FragmentFactory change that, and what breaks if you pass dependencies through a custom constructor?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It exposes understanding of how the framework recreates fragments after config change and process death.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The system recreates fragments reflectively from the class name saved in the instance state, with no knowledge of your arguments. By default it needs a public no-arg constructor, and state comes from arguments and saved state. Since fragment 1.1 I can set a FragmentFactory on the FragmentManager to construct fragments with dependencies. It must be installed before restoration happens, that is before super.onCreate() in the Activity, or restoration throws Fragment.InstantiationException."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When the Activity is recreated with a saved state, FragmentManager.restoreSaveState iterates the saved FragmentState entries and calls fragmentFactory.instantiate(classLoader, className) for each, then restores arguments and saved state into the new instance. The framework only knows the class name, so:

  • Without a factory: Class.getConstructor() with no args; missing it fails at restore time (not at creation time) with androidx.fragment.app.Fragment$InstantiationException: Unable to instantiate fragment ...: could not find Fragment constructor. That is why a bug can pass all manual flows and crash only after rotation or process death.
  • With a factory: you construct with dependencies; but the factory must be available at restoration. Set it in onCreate before super.onCreate(savedInstanceState). A factory that references Activity-bound objects must rebuild them for the new Activity.
  • Dependencies in constructors are not saved; any data the fragment needs (ids, modes) still goes into arguments. Dependencies are services, not state.
  • DI frameworks: Hilt @AndroidEntryPoint fragments use field injection and need no custom factory; Koin/Dagger-assisted setups often use a factory. Keep arguments for state in all cases.
  • Fragments also have a Fragment(@LayoutRes int) constructor for layout inflation convenience.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class AppFragmentFactory(private val repo: Repo) : FragmentFactory() {
    override fun instantiate(cl: ClassLoader, className: String): Fragment =
        when (loadFragmentClass(cl, className)) {
            ProfileFragment::class.java -> ProfileFragment(repo)
            else -> super.instantiate(cl, className)
        }
}

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        supportFragmentManager.fragmentFactory = AppFragmentFactory(Repo()) // BEFORE super
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    }
}

class ProfileFragment(private val repo: Repo) : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    companion object {
        fun newInstance(id: String) = ProfileFragment(Repo()).apply { arguments = bundleOf("id" to id) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fragment has constructor parameters but no factory is installed: works until the first recreation.
  • Setting the factory after super.onCreate, so restored fragments are built with the default factory.
  • Storing the data (not services) in the constructor, which is lost on recreation.
  • Setting the factory only on the Activity's manager while a child manager also needs it (child managers inherit from parent in recent versions; verify for your fragment version).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test this? → Use "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill to force recreation, or FragmentScenario/ActivityScenario.recreate().
  2. Hilt and constructor injection? → Hilt uses members injection for fragments; constructor injection into fragments is not supported by default.
  3. What about DialogFragments? → Same instantiation path; a constructor with dependencies fails identically.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "fragments need an empty constructor". Senior explains why (reflective restoration by name), when it fails (restore, not create), and the ordering requirement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash appeared only in crash logs from users who returned after hours; QA never saw it because they never triggered process death. The fragment had gained a repository constructor parameter.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (900k DAU) has a feed Fragment that opens article detail via replace + addToBackStack. After users open 4-5 articles and press back, memory climbs; Crashlytics shows 1.4% of sessions end in OOM on 2 GB devices. LeakCanary on a debug build reports: "FeedFragment received Fragment#onDestroyView() callback ... leaking: DestroyedView". Code:

class FeedFragment : Fragment() {
    private lateinit var binding: FragmentFeedBinding
    private val vm: FeedViewModel by viewModels()
    private val adapter = FeedAdapter { id -> openArticle(id) }

    override fun onCreateView(i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle?): View {
        binding = FragmentFeedBinding.inflate(i, c, false)
        return binding.root
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        binding.list.adapter = adapter
        vm.items.observe(this) { adapter.submitList(it) }
        lifecycleScope.launch { vm.refreshing.collect { binding.swipe.isRefreshing = it } }
    }
}

Red herrings: the team suspects Glide caching and the feed's image sizes; heap dumps show the dominators are bitmaps.
questions.promptHtml: Find what is wrong, explain the memory growth mechanism, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Glide is caching too much; lower the cache size or call clear()." Or "add onDestroyView { binding = null }" without noticing lateinit, the adapter, or the observer scope issues.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the OOM correlate with back-stack depth? (confirms view retention vs image cache). Are there other Fragment-scoped fields holding views? Which FeedAdapter constructor captures what? Is it also seen on devices with larger heaps (just delayed)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that nulls the binding and clears the adapter; as a stop-gap, lower the number of items prefetched and Glide onTrimMemory handling. Not a rollout rollback, since the leak existed before.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Fragment on the back stack retains binding -> view tree -> loaded bitmaps (most likely, matches LeakCanary). (b) observe(this) and lifecycleScope collection survive onDestroyView and keep calling into the dead binding, and also stack observers each return. (c) Adapter holds ViewHolders (views) when attached to the list and is a field of the fragment. (d) Glide cache size; the dominators are bitmaps, but they are reachable only through the leaked views.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary's leak trace (path FeedFragment.binding -> root -> ... -> Bitmap); heap dump in Android Studio profiler after navigating 5 deep and back, filter on FeedFragment and count FragmentFeedBinding instances; Fragment.viewLifecycleOwner use grep; count observers with a debug log in the LiveData observer.
  5. Root cause: lateinit var binding is never cleared, so while the fragment instance sits on the back stack (state CREATED), it keeps the whole view tree reachable, including RecyclerView recycled pools with bitmaps. 5 stacked feeds x ~12 MB of bound images = 60 MB, large relative to a 256 MB largeHeap-less limit on a 2 GB device. Also observers use the fragment lifecycle, so they live while the view is gone and stack on every return, calling adapter.submitList and binding.swipe on stale views.
  6. Fix:
class FeedFragment : Fragment() {
    private var _binding: FragmentFeedBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!
    private val vm: FeedViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreateView(i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle?): View {
        _binding = FragmentFeedBinding.inflate(i, c, false)
        return binding.root
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        val adapter = FeedAdapter { id -> openArticle(id) } // created per view
        binding.list.adapter = adapter
        vm.items.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { adapter.submitList(it) }
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                vm.refreshing.collect { binding.swipe.isRefreshing = it }
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        binding.list.adapter = null
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}
  1. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug builds and in CI instrumentation tests that navigate and assert no retained objects; custom lint (or detekt rule) banning lateinit var binding in Fragments and observe(this) in onViewCreated; a code-review checklist item "view-scoped things use viewLifecycleOwner and are released in onDestroyView".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just shrink the image cache (treats a symptom, hurts scrolling); not use largeHeap (hides the leak, makes GC pauses longer); not replace instead of back-stack (changes UX).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would setRetainInstance(true) help? → No; deprecated, and it would keep the instance (and the leaked views) even longer.
  • The leak persists after the fix on a screen with a MapView? → Map/WebView need their own lifecycle calls and onDestroyView cleanup.
  • How do you prove the fix in numbers? → Heap dump before/after navigating 5 deep; FragmentFeedBinding count must drop to 1 and Java heap back to baseline within a GC.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shopping app's OOM rate dropped from 1.1% to 0.2% after a one-line _binding = null rollout; the earlier team had spent two sprints tuning the image loader.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames image library, proposes largeHeap or bigger caches.
  • Hire: finds the binding leak and fixes with _binding = null.
  • Strong hire: also fixes observers/lifecycleScope, adapter, quantifies retention, and adds automated prevention.

questions.promptHtml: What are the common pitfalls with DialogFragment, and why prefer it over showing AlertDialog directly from an Activity or Fragment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dialogs are everywhere; crashes after state saved and leaked window errors are classic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A DialogFragment is a Fragment whose view lives in a dialog window, so the FragmentManager recreates it on rotation and process restoration, while a raw AlertDialog.show() is destroyed with the Activity and throws WindowLeaked if not dismissed. Pitfalls: show() is a commit, so it throws IllegalStateException if state is saved; dismiss() the same, so use dismissAllowingStateLoss() when needed; keep listeners out of constructors and use the Fragment Result API; check for an existing instance before showing; use onCreateDialog or onCreateView, not both unintentionally; and use viewLifecycleOwner carefully, since it exists only when you supply a view."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Creation: onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState) returns the Dialog (typical for MaterialAlertDialogBuilder); onCreateView supplies content for a custom layout. If you override onCreateDialog and not onCreateView, the fragment has no view, and in older Fragment versions accessing viewLifecycleOwner throws; recent versions provide a view lifecycle only when a content view exists (verify for your version, and avoid depending on it).
  • show(fragmentManager, tag) executes commit(). showNow exists for sync. Both throw after state save. dismiss() uses a back stack pop or commit(); dismissAllowingStateLoss() skips the check.
  • Duplicate dialogs: rapid taps call show() twice; check findFragmentByTag(tag) == null or isStateSaved. After rotation the system already restores the dialog; showing again in onCreate stacks two.
  • Callbacks: never pass a lambda or the Activity through a constructor (lost on recreation or leaks); use setFragmentResult or an interface resolved in onAttach/onCreate via parentFragment/requireActivity casting.
  • Cancel: use isCancelable = false on the DialogFragment (not dialog.setCancelable, which gets reset on recreate).
  • Sizing/width: set in onStart() (window exists) via dialog.window?.setLayout.
  • Theme: setStyle(STYLE_NORMAL, R.style.MyDialogTheme) before onCreateDialog.
  • setTargetFragment is deprecated; same with onActivityResult flow.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ConfirmDialog : DialogFragment() {
    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog =
        MaterialAlertDialogBuilder(requireContext())
            .setTitle(requireArguments().getString("title"))
            .setPositiveButton(android.R.string.ok) { _, _ ->
                parentFragmentManager.setFragmentResult("confirm", bundleOf("ok" to true))
            }
            .setNegativeButton(android.R.string.cancel, null)
            .create()

    companion object {
        const val TAG = "confirm"
        fun show(fm: FragmentManager, title: String) {
            if (fm.isStateSaved || fm.findFragmentByTag(TAG) != null) return
            ConfirmDialog().apply { arguments = bundleOf("title" to title) }.show(fm, TAG)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling dismiss() in an async callback after the user backgrounded the app.
  • Overriding both onCreateDialog and onCreateView and getting a blank dialog (the Dialog's content view is replaced).
  • Holding a lateinit listener assigned from the caller; null after recreation.
  • Showing a DialogFragment from a ViewModel event consumed on every start.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not AlertDialog directly? → Dies with the Activity (WindowLeaked), no state restoration, and rotation shows nothing or leaks.
  2. What happens to a dialog during rotation? → It is dismissed and recreated by the FragmentManager from saved state.
  3. How do you avoid showing the same dialog twice from rapid taps? → Check existing fragment by tag, disable the trigger, or model the dialog as UI state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use DialogFragment so it survives rotation". Senior lists commit/state-loss paths, callback handling via the Result API, lifecycle owner subtleties and de-duplication.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "App crashed: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" cluster all pointed at ConfirmDialog.dismiss() from a retrofit callback.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (2.5M DAU) shipped version 8.12 on Monday. By Wednesday Crashlytics shows a new top crash affecting 0.6% of sessions (about 15k users/day), concentrated on Android 9-13, mostly on the order tracking screen:

Fatal Exception: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.checkStateLoss(FragmentManager.java:1856)
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.enqueueAction(FragmentManager.java:1894)
    at androidx.fragment.app.BackStackRecord.commitInternal(BackStackRecord.java:329)
    at androidx.fragment.app.BackStackRecord.commit(BackStackRecord.java:294)
    at com.app.tracking.TrackingActivity$onOrderUpdate$1.invokeSuspend(TrackingActivity.kt:88)

Release notes: migrated the order tracking from polling to a WebSocket; on ORDER_DELIVERED the Activity replaces the map fragment with a "Rate your order" fragment. Red herring: the crash rate also moved on devices without the new feature flag, because a library bump (Fragment 1.5 -> 1.6) shipped in the same release.
questions.promptHtml: How do you triage, stop the bleeding, find the root cause, and prevent the class of bug?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace commit with commitAllowingStateLoss." This silences the crash but can restore a stale screen after process death, and does not address why the events arrive when the Activity is stopped.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the crash correlated with the flag or the library bump (staged rollout split in Crashlytics)? What is the foreground/background state at crash time (breadcrumb logs)? Does the socket stay open when the app is backgrounded? Which API levels (onSaveInstanceState ordering differs: after onStop on 28+, before it earlier)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side feature flag off for the WebSocket path (polling returns), halting the staged rollout at current percentage. A client hotfix: guard the transaction with isStateSaved.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The socket callback arrives while the Activity is stopped and state already saved. (b) Callback runs during the short window between onSaveInstanceState and onResume on older APIs. (c) Fragment library bump added stricter checks. (d) Two events racing (DELIVERED + PAID). Red herring: library bump is only coincident; crash stack points at app code.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with adb shell am start the screen, press Home, then replay a socket message with a debug server; Developer option "Don't keep activities"; add Lifecycle.currentState and isStateSaved to the crash custom keys; compare crash rates between flag-on and flag-off cohorts.
  5. Root cause: The WebSocket listener runs on a background thread, posts to Main, and calls commit() regardless of the Activity's state. A user who pockets the phone mid-delivery stops the Activity; onSaveInstanceState has run; the next message calls commit(), which throws. Polling used to be tied to repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), which hid the issue.
  6. Fix: short term, if (supportFragmentManager.isStateSaved) pending = DELIVERED else show(). Long term, make the screen state-driven:
// ViewModel
val screen: StateFlow<TrackingScreen> // Tracking, Rate

// Activity
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.screen.collect { render(it) } // applied only while STARTED; latest state replayed on return
    }
}

The state is retained in the ViewModel (and SavedStateHandle if it must survive death), so the rating screen appears when the user returns. 7. Prevention: Policy: no fragment transactions or navigate() from async callbacks; only from STARTED-scoped collectors. Detekt/lint rule against commit() inside enqueue/launch lambdas; instrumented test that backgrounds the Activity, emits a state change, and resumes; log Lifecycle.State as a Crashlytics key. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use commitAllowingStateLoss for the rating screen: on process death, the user would restore to the map screen though the order is delivered (inconsistent, though mild). It is acceptable only for purely cosmetic overlays. I would not retain pending transactions in a static singleton either (leaks, loses on process death).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The product wants a push notification if the app is stopped when delivered → Handle in FCM/notification path; do not rely on UI.
  • What if the Activity is in the foreground but a dialog (Activity paused) is open? → Paused but state not saved; commit() works; verify with isStateSaved.
  • The state-driven approach shows a rating screen the moment the user returns; is that OK? → Product decision; consume once and persist "rated" to avoid re-show.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A booking app spent a sprint toggling commitAllowingStateLoss across 30 call sites; the cleaner fix was one StateFlow and a single render function, and the crash class disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: switches to commitAllowingStateLoss and closes the ticket.
  • Hire: explains the state-saved window and guards with lifecycle checks.
  • Strong hire: separates the red herring, redesigns around state, adds tests and metrics, and discusses process-death consistency.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app uses Navigation component (single Activity, NavHostFragment, Navigation 2.7) with a 3-step "Add beneficiary" form: Details -> Verify -> Review. Product says: "When the user goes back from Review to Details, the form must still be filled in." QA reports that on back, the name field is filled but the dropdown selection and a RecyclerView of suggested banks reset to the top, and sometimes the whole form is empty after the user took a call (app in background ~20 min). Typical device mix: 55% mid-range 4 GB, 30% 2-3 GB. Red herring: someone suggests using hide()/show() fragments instead of Navigation to "keep the views".
questions.promptHtml: The requirement says "still be filled in". How do you clarify it, and how do you design it so it works for rotation, back navigation, and the 20-minute background case?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Navigation destroys fragments on back, so switch to hide/show" or "make fields static". Misses that nothing about the view survives, and that the 20-minute case is process death.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should data survive only back navigation, or also rotation, app kill and process death? Should it survive a full flow exit and re-entry (draft persisted)? Is any field sensitive (account number) so we must not persist it? What counts as "filled": typed text, selection, scroll position? How long is a draft valid?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the reported bug, move the form values out of the views and into one ViewModel; this fixes back navigation immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Only views with ids restore text; a custom dropdown and selection are held in view state only. (b) With Navigation's FragmentNavigator, the previous destination's view is destroyed (the fragment stays CREATED), so view-only state is lost unless saved. (c) The empty form after 20 minutes is process death: ViewModel is gone. (d) RecyclerView scroll reset because the adapter is re-attached and data loads async.
  4. How I'd verify each: Navigate forward and back with the Layout Inspector/Debug logs on onDestroyView/onViewCreated; enable "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill <pkg> after backgrounding to simulate the call; check the NavBackStackEntry lifecycle via findNavController().currentBackStackEntry.
  5. Root cause: Navigation's fragment navigator replaces fragments, destroying their view each navigation. Only the instance, arguments, ViewModel, and framework-saved view state with ids survive. The requirement was implemented as "views keep what they have", which holds only if everything is stored in view state.
  6. Fix: State layering. Form model in a ViewModel scoped to the nav graph (navGraphViewModels(R.id.add_beneficiary)), with a SavedStateHandle for the primitive fields so process death restores them; the fragment binds to it with viewLifecycleOwner and renders; scroll position via StateRestorationPolicy / saving LayoutManager state in the ViewModel. For persistence beyond that, write a draft to local storage (excluding sensitive fields) with a TTL.
class BeneficiaryFormViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    var name: String
        get() = handle["name"] ?: ""
        set(v) { handle["name"] = v }
    val bankId = handle.getStateFlow("bankId", -1L) // lifecycle-viewmodel-savedstate 2.5+
    fun selectBank(id: Long) { handle["bankId"] = id }
}
  1. Prevention: Navigation instrumentation test: fill, go forward, back, rotate, am kill, relaunch; assert the form. A convention that screens must render purely from ViewModel state plus restored saved state ("no view is a source of truth").
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use hide/show: it pins every view tree in memory (on 2 GB phones that is expensive), keeps hidden fragments in RESUMED unless setMaxLifecycle is used, and still loses everything on process death. I would not persist sensitive fields to disk; for those, re-ask the user after process death and say so in the UI.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can the graph-scoped ViewModel crash? → Yes, if requested when the graph is not on the back stack (IllegalArgumentException); initialize inside destinations of that graph only.
  • Product wants the draft restored after a day → Persist to Room/DataStore with a TTL; clear on submit/cancel.
  • Why not rely on the fragment's saved view state alone? → Only views with ids restore automatically, and only simple state; async lists and custom views do not.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A KYC flow lost 3% of completions at the document-upload step because users got interrupted by the camera app and returned to an empty form; adding a SavedStateHandle-backed ViewModel recovered most of it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests hide/show or statics without clarifying.
  • Hire: moves state to ViewModel and handles rotation.
  • Strong hire: layers ViewModel, saved state and persistent draft, clarifies sensitivity and TTL, and tests process death.

questions.promptHtml: How does FragmentStateAdapter manage fragments in a ViewPager2? Which lifecycle state does each page's fragment reach, what is offscreenPageLimit, and what do you need to watch out for when the ViewPager2 lives inside a Fragment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tabs are in nearly every app; mistakes cause wasted work in invisible tabs, leaks, and state loss.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "ViewPager2 is built on RecyclerView; FragmentStateAdapter creates a Fragment per page and attaches it to the pager item's container. Only the current page's fragment is RESUMED; neighbours are held at STARTED via setMaxLifecycle, so onResume is a reliable 'this tab is current' signal. By default, pages beyond the RecyclerView cache are destroyed and their fragment state is saved (f#<itemId> keys), then restored when scrolled back. Inside a Fragment, I must pass childFragmentManager and viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle, and clear the adapter in onDestroyView."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• FragmentStateAdapter(FragmentManager, Lifecycle) (three constructors: FragmentActivity, Fragment, or manager+lifecycle). The Fragment constructor uses childFragmentManager and lifecycle of the fragment, not the view lifecycle; when the pager is in the view of a Fragment that can be put on the back stack, I prefer manager + viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle so the adapter's observers die with the view (verify against the adapter version and what the constructor wires).
  • Page fragments are attached when the RecyclerView item (a FrameLayout) attaches, and detached on recycle. offscreenPageLimit = n (default OFFSCREEN_PAGE_LIMIT_DEFAULT) keeps n pages each side laid out and created. With n = 1, 3 fragments exist and 3 onCreateViews ran; with the default, only the visible one plus partially visible pages during a scroll.
  • Lifecycle caps: the current page gets RESUMED; others are capped at STARTED (FragmentTransaction.setMaxLifecycle, fragment 1.1+). This replaced the old setUserVisibleHint and BEHAVIOR_RESUME_ONLY_CURRENT_FRAGMENT of FragmentPagerAdapter (deprecated).
  • Stable ids: override getItemId and containsItem if pages can be reordered or deleted, or the adapter will reuse or lose fragments.
  • Saved state: saveState() stores Fragment.SavedState for fragments not currently in the manager under keys prefixed f# and s#; the pager itself saves its position. Large per-page state counts against the 1 MB Binder transaction (see the saved-state chunk).
  • Orientation, nested scrolling (a horizontal RecyclerView in a page steals swipes unless handled) and userInputEnabled are pager-level.
  • ViewPager2 is final and does not accept PagerAdapter; FragmentStatePagerAdapter is deprecated.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class HostFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_host) {
    private var _binding: FragmentHostBinding? = null

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        val b = FragmentHostBinding.bind(view).also { _binding = it }
        b.pager.adapter = TabsAdapter(childFragmentManager, viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle)
        TabLayoutMediator(b.tabs, b.pager) { tab, pos -> tab.text = titles[pos] }.attach()
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        _binding?.pager?.adapter = null // adapter holds fragment manager refs and observers
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}

class TabsAdapter(fm: FragmentManager, lc: Lifecycle) : FragmentStateAdapter(fm, lc) {
    override fun getItemCount() = 3
    override fun createFragment(position: Int): Fragment = when (position) {
        0 -> FeedFragment(); 1 -> SearchFragment(); else -> ProfileFragment()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using requireActivity().supportFragmentManager when the pager is nested, which leaves page fragments hanging after the host's view is destroyed.
  • Doing data loading in onViewCreated/onStart of every tab, so all neighbours fetch; put "tab became current" work in onResume.
  • Using Fragment instances stored in a list by the adapter; the pager recreates them.
  • Setting offscreenPageLimit to the number of tabs to "avoid reload" (5 heavy tabs in memory).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do I load data for a tab only when it becomes visible? → Observe or load in onResume (current page only), or use a pager-selected callback to tell a shared ViewModel.
  2. What happens to a tab scrolled far away? → Fragment is removed; state is saved; on return it is recreated with onCreateView and the saved state.
  3. Why would a tab's Fragment ViewModel be re-created? → The fragment was removed permanently from the child manager (not just detached) and had no retained store; scope data to the host if it must persist.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "FragmentStateAdapter for ViewPager2". Senior knows maxLifecycle semantics, offscreen limit costs, state keys and stable ids, nested-manager and lifecycle choices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home screen fired five parallel API calls on cold start because every tab loaded in onStart; moving the first load into onResume of the current page cut p95 start-to-content by 30%.

questions.promptHtml: What actually happens between calling commit() and the fragment's onCreateView running? Explain how the FragmentManager schedules transactions, what setMaxLifecycle and setReorderingAllowed do, and why a fragment added in onCreate might not be created yet.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about ordering bugs ("my fragment is null right after commit") rather than cargo-culting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "commit() does not run the transaction. It adds a BackStackRecord to a pending list and posts an Runnable to the host's main-thread handler. When it runs, the manager executes the ops, and each fragment's state is moved toward the host's current state by a FragmentStateManager: attach, create, create view, activity-created, start, resume, never above what the host or the setMaxLifecycle cap allows. So right after commit(), findFragmentByTag returns null. commitNow() or executePendingTransactions() run it synchronously."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pipeline:

commit()
  -> BackStackRecord added to mPendingActions
  -> handler.post(execPendingActions)             // async, same Looper
  -> execPendingActions: collect records, optional optimization (reordering)
  -> executeOps: add/remove/replace/hide/show/setMaxLifecycle -> mark target state
  -> moveToState(): FragmentStateManager.moveToExpectedState()
        INITIALIZED -> attach -> create -> createView -> start -> resume

Key properties:

  • Fragment state is bounded by min(host state, maxLifecycle cap). During Activity.onCreate, the manager is in CREATED, so a fragment committed there reaches CREATED/view-created only as the Activity progresses (onStart moves it to STARTED); it also means onViewCreated runs later than your onCreate returns.
  • setReorderingAllowed(true) allows the manager to reorder and optimize operations across records (e.g. skipping fragments that are added and removed within the same batch, so they never reach onCreateView), and is required for transitions to play correctly with state changes. It also changes callback ordering, so do not depend on a precise sequence.
  • setMaxLifecycle(fragment, state) (1.1+) caps the fragment's state without removing it; allowed CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED; INITIALIZED/DESTROYED are not allowed (throws). ViewPager2 uses it for page visibility.
  • Synchronous variants: commitNow and executePendingTransactions; the latter cannot be called while another execution is in progress (throws IllegalStateException: FragmentManager is already executing transactions).
  • popBackStack() also posts; popBackStackImmediate() is sync and returns a boolean.
  • Entering and exit animation/transition effects delay fragment destruction ("special effects"): a removed fragment's view stays attached and the fragment stays in a pre-destroy state until the animation ends (onDestroyView is deferred; Fragment.getView still returns a view). Handled via SpecialEffectsController.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
supportFragmentManager.commit { add(R.id.container, DetailFragment(), "detail") }
val f = supportFragmentManager.findFragmentByTag("detail") // null here (async commit)

supportFragmentManager.commitNow { add(R.id.container, DetailFragment(), "detail") }
val g = supportFragmentManager.findFragmentByTag("detail") // non-null now

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the result of findFragmentById immediately after commit().
  • Wrapping transactions in executePendingTransactions() calls "to be safe" inside lifecycle callbacks.
  • Assuming onCreateView runs on the same stack frame as commit.
  • Using commitNow with addToBackStack, which throws.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can onViewCreated of a fragment added in Activity.onCreate run after onStart of the Activity? → The manager brings fragments to the host state step by step; in particular after the transaction posts or when the host's state advances.
  2. What does the manager do if you commit twice in one frame? → Both records are queued and executed together in one execPendingActions pass, possibly optimized when reordering is allowed.
  3. How does the fragment know the host moved to STOPPED? → The Activity dispatches lifecycle events to the manager (dispatchStop etc.), which moves all fragments' states down.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "commit is async, commitNow is sync". Senior describes the queue, state capping, reordering effects and animation deferral, and uses it to reason about bugs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky UI test failed because it asserted on a fragment right after commit(); the fix was commitNow in test setup and IdlingResource in the app flow.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly is saved and restored for a Fragment across configuration change and across process death? Where do arguments, onSaveInstanceState, view state, ViewModel, and the FragmentManager's own state fit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Process-death bugs in fragments are the most common "only on real users' phones" crash.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three layers. The FragmentManager saves which fragments exist, their class names, ids, tags, arguments, back stack, and each fragment's onSaveInstanceState Bundle, as part of the Activity's saved state, and recreates the instances reflectively. View state for views with ids is saved separately and restored in onViewStateRestored. ViewModels survive configuration changes but not process death, so important data needs SavedStateHandle or persistent storage. Everything saved passes through a Binder transaction with about a 1 MB shared budget."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers:

Thing Config change (rotation) Process death
Fragment instance fields Lost (new instance) Lost
arguments Restored Restored
onSaveInstanceState(outState) Bundle Restored (onCreate(saved)) Restored
View state (ids needed) Restored Restored
FragmentManager back stack/tags Restored Restored
ViewModel Survives Lost
SavedStateHandle Survives Restored
Static/singleton Survives Lost (process re-created)

Mechanics:

  • On FragmentActivity.onSaveInstanceState, the manager writes FragmentManagerState (active fragments each by FragmentState: class name, mWho unique id, tag, container id, args, mSavedFragmentState, etc.) under a key such as android:support:fragments in the Activity's Bundle. The Activity's Bundle goes to system_server (ActivityTaskManager) for later restore.
  • The Fragment's own bundle is produced by Fragment.onSaveInstanceState and also by registered SavedStateRegistry providers (the Fragment is a SavedStateRegistryOwner; SavedStateHandle is wired through it).
  • Views: when the view is being destroyed, saveHierarchyState writes a SparseArray<Parcelable> keyed by view id (so ids must be stable and unique; RecyclerView saves layout state if the adapter policy allows).
  • setRetainInstance(true) (deprecated since Fragment 1.3) kept an instance across rotation; ViewModel replaces it.
  • registerForActivityResult launchers should be registered as property initializers or in onCreate so they exist before STARTED; they re-register by key after recreation.
  • The Bundle size limit: all saved state in a process goes into one Binder transaction (1 MB buffer shared, exceeding it gives TransactionTooLargeException on API 24+, previously a silent loss; see the process-death chunk).
  • Fragments on the back stack are saved even though they have no views, so large objects in onSaveInstanceState for many stacked fragments add up.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CartFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_cart) {
    private val vm: CartViewModel by viewModels()
    private var selectedId: Long = -1

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        selectedId = savedInstanceState?.getLong("selectedId", -1) ?: -1
    }

    override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
        outState.putLong("selectedId", selectedId) // small ids only, never lists of models
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing a list of domain models in onSaveInstanceState instead of an id and re-querying.
  • Relying on the ViewModel alone for user input.
  • Views without ids (or duplicate ids across included layouts) causing wrong or no restoration.
  • Testing only rotation, which preserves ViewModel and hides process-death bugs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test restoration? → "Don't keep activities", adb shell am kill after backgrounding, FragmentScenario.recreate() for config change, and instrumentation for am kill flows.
  2. What is restored first, fragments or the Activity's views? → The Activity's onCreate(savedInstanceState) restores the manager state when super.onCreate runs; fragments begin recreation then.
  3. Why can restoring cause a crash on a back-stacked fragment you cannot see? → Its onCreate and arguments are required to be valid even when its view is not created, so missing arguments throw at restore.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use onSaveInstanceState and ViewModel". Senior has the table, knows ids for view state, SavedStateHandle, sizes, and test methods.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a deploy, crash reports from users returning after hours with "requireArguments() not found"; a code path created the fragment without arguments and only surfaced on restore.

questions.promptHtml: How should a Fragment contribute to the toolbar menu today? Why was setHasOptionsMenu/onCreateOptionsMenu deprecated, and what does MenuProvider change about lifecycle?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Menus are a leftover legacy API with lifecycle pitfalls; a good answer shows knowledge of modern host contracts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "setHasOptionsMenu(true) and the Fragment onCreateOptionsMenu callbacks were deprecated in Fragment 1.5.0 in favour of MenuProvider. The Activity (a MenuHost, from Activity 1.4.0) lets me add providers with addMenuProvider(provider, viewLifecycleOwner, Lifecycle.State.RESUMED). The menu items are then active only while the lifecycle owner is at that state and removed automatically when it's destroyed, which avoids the stale items and double-inflation seen with fragment-owned callbacks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Old model: the Activity's onCreateOptionsMenu iterated over fragments with hasOptionsMenu, and every fragment state change called invalidateOptionsMenu. Problems: tied to Fragment instance lifecycle (not view), unclear ordering between fragments, and no per-state control. Also interacted badly with hide() and nested fragments.

New model:

  • MenuHost (implemented by ComponentActivity) holds MenuProviders: onCreateMenu, onPrepareMenu, onMenuItemSelected, onMenuClosed.
  • addMenuProvider(provider) always active; addMenuProvider(provider, owner) active while owner is at least RESUMED (default state); addMenuProvider(provider, owner, state) chooses the state. When the owner reaches DESTROYED, the provider is removed.
  • Fragments should pass viewLifecycleOwner (their menu relates to the view); using the fragment's own lifecycle re-adds a provider on each onViewCreated and leaves stale providers on the back stack, exactly like the LiveData duplicate-observer problem.
  • Menu changes: call requireActivity().invalidateMenu() to refresh state (e.g. enable/disable items), then onPrepareMenu runs.
  • Activity-level toolbar (setSupportActionBar) vs Material Toolbar inside the fragment: with a toolbar inside the fragment's layout, you can inflate directly with toolbar.inflateMenu(...) and set setOnMenuItemClickListener, which keeps the menu inside the view's lifecycle without the Activity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    requireActivity().addMenuProvider(object : MenuProvider {
        override fun onCreateMenu(menu: Menu, inflater: MenuInflater) {
            inflater.inflate(R.menu.detail_menu, menu)
        }
