        override fun onMenuItemSelected(item: MenuItem): Boolean = when (item.itemId) {
            R.id.action_share -> { share(); true }
            else -> false
        }
    }, viewLifecycleOwner, Lifecycle.State.RESUMED)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing this (the Fragment) as owner so providers accumulate while on the back stack.
  • Forgetting invalidateMenu() after state changes, leaving stale enablement.
  • Handling item clicks in both the old callback and the provider.
  • Referencing views inside the provider after the view is gone (provider is removed by the owner state; ensure it uses viewLifecycleOwner).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about nested fragments? → Providers are Activity-level; each registers with its own viewLifecycleOwner so only visible ones are active.
  2. How does this relate to Compose? → Compose UIs use a TopAppBar with actions directly; MenuProvider is only for View-based Toolbar/ActionBar integration (details in the Compose chunk).
  3. Does the order of providers matter? → They are invoked in registration order; avoid relying on it, and give items distinct ids/orders.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "setHasOptionsMenu(true)". Senior knows the deprecation version, host/owner/state parameters, and the viewLifecycleOwner rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A detail screen showed two "Share" icons after navigating forward and back because a menu was re-inflated for the same Fragment instance without removing the previous provider.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (1.2M DAU) has a ChatActivity that hosts a ChatFragment and a ComposerFragment. Support tickets: "after rotating, the message list is shown twice, overlapping, and sending a message inserts it into only one of them." Crash-free is fine; no stack trace. Reported 8x more on tablets and foldables (which rotate and resize often). Code:

class ChatActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_chat) // contains FrameLayout @+id/chat_container, @+id/composer_container
        supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction()
            .add(R.id.chat_container, ChatFragment.newInstance(intent.getStringExtra("chatId")!!))
            .add(R.id.composer_container, ComposerFragment())
            .commit()
    }
}

Red herrings: someone suspects RecyclerView item animator duplication and the new Paging library bump.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, why only after recreation, and how do you fix it robustly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use replace instead of add" without understanding why a fresh add is wrong on restore, or "set configChanges to avoid rotation recreation", which hides rather than fixes (and breaks on process death and locale changes).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce after process death as well as rotation? Is it only with add, and does it exist in both fragments? What does adb shell dumpsys activity <activity> show for fragments in the manager? Any android:configChanges in the manifest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix with a savedInstanceState == null guard so the transaction runs only on first creation; it takes minutes and is safe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) On recreation the FragmentManager has already restored both fragments from saved state, then onCreate adds a second pair; (b) the FrameLayouts are in the layout, so both fragments' views are attached to the same containers, overlapping; (c) RecyclerView animator duplicates (unlikely: the symptom is two lists); (d) Paging bump (unrelated, as the duplicates show on a clean tree).
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys activity top | grep -A20 "Active Fragments" before and after rotation (expect 2 then 4 active fragments); Layout Inspector shows two RecyclerViews in the container; log supportFragmentManager.fragments.size in onCreate with savedInstanceState != null; reproduce with FragmentScenario/ActivityScenario.recreate() or "Don't keep activities".
  5. Root cause: super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) restores the previous fragments automatically (before your code). The onCreate code unconditionally adds new ones, so there are four fragments. The restored ChatFragment and the new one both render into the same container, and each owns its own ViewModel scope (separate by viewModels() instances in two fragment instances), so a sent message appears only in one list.
  6. Fix:
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_chat)
    if (savedInstanceState == null) { // the manager restores existing fragments itself
        supportFragmentManager.commit {
            setReorderingAllowed(true)
            add(R.id.chat_container, ChatFragment.newInstance(intent.getStringExtra("chatId")!!))
            add(R.id.composer_container, ComposerFragment())
        }
    }
}

Even better: declare them in XML with FragmentContainerView android:name="..." and pass arguments via android:tag/intent in the fragment, or use Navigation. If the Activity can be relaunched with a different chatId via onNewIntent (singleTop), handle with an explicit replace. 7. Prevention: ActivityScenario.recreate() instrumentation test asserting fragments.size == 2; lint/detekt rule or code-review rule: "transactions in onCreate must be guarded"; prefer FragmentContainerView with android:name for static layouts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not configChanges="orientation|screenSize..." as the fix: it avoids recreation for rotation but not for process death, locale, dark mode or font scale, and foldable resizes. Not replace + a tag lookup everywhere as a patch for logic that should only run once. Not removing fragments manually at the start of onCreate (flicker, churn).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• With the guard in place, a chat opened via a new notification (singleTop, onNewIntent) shows the old chat → The guard prevents re-adding; handle onNewIntent by replacing with a new fragment/loading the new id into the ViewModel.
  • Does FragmentContainerView android:name have the same issue? → No; the manager restores the declared fragment and does not re-add on recreation.
  • Could the duplicates cause a crash? → Yes, if IDs collide in view state restoration or two ViewModels fire the same event twice.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tablet-first product shipped the bug for two releases because QA tested portrait phones; it was found only when a foldable partner reported it, and the guard fixed 100% of reports.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames RecyclerView or locks orientation.
  • Hire: finds the missing savedInstanceState == null guard and explains auto-restoration.
  • Strong hire: also verifies via dumpsys, covers onNewIntent, tests recreation automatically, and explains why configChanges is a trap.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for a ride-hailing app (4M DAU). Release 5.40 had 0.9% crash-affected sessions, 70% on one signature across Android 8-14:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment RideSummaryFragment{...} not attached to a context.
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.requireContext(Fragment.java:...)
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getResources(Fragment.java:...)
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getString(Fragment.java:...)
    at com.app.ride.RideSummaryFragment.showFare$lambda(RideSummaryFragment.kt:142)

and a second, 20% signature java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment RideSummaryFragment not associated with a fragment manager. from parentFragmentManager. The fare is fetched with a callback-based client; the screen is popped by users in ~12% of cases before the fare returns (p95 fare latency is 2.8 s on 3G). The fix attempted in 5.40.1 wrapped the calls in if (isAdded); crash rate fell by only 25%.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: why did the first fix not work, what is the real root cause, and what systemic changes do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add isAdded checks everywhere." Check-then-act on a main thread callback is OK, but it hides logic errors and misses coroutine/Flow continuation, getActivity() ?: return patterns and dialogs; the crash persisted for other paths.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: In the remaining 75%, is the call inside a lambda posted to a different thread/handler (isAdded checked on one thread, used on another)? Is isAdded the right check (what about view != null or viewLifecycleOwner)? Do the crashes occur at getString(), requireActivity(), parentFragmentManager or binding? Which code is callback-based vs coroutine-based?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the affected prefetch path via remote config, hotfix the top three call sites to resolve strings via an app-level Application context for text that doesn't need an Activity theme.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Async callbacks outlive the fragment: no cancellation. (b) Some code reads isAdded but then continues to use binding, which is cleared at onDestroyView (added but view gone: isAdded is true between onAttach and onDetach, including when the fragment is on the back stack without a view); (c) callbacks hop threads (check on a background thread, use on main later); (d) parentFragmentManager called from a Handler.postDelayed after the pop.
  4. How I'd verify each: Search crash stack tops by call site; reproduce by throttling to 3G in Charles/Network Profiler and popping within 2 s; add breadcrumbs for viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.currentState and isAdded, isDetached, view != null at crash time; review diffs for callbacks not tied to lifecycle.
  5. Root cause: The work was not owned by a lifecycle. The callback keeps a strong reference to the Fragment and fires after onDetach, when mHost is null; Fragment methods like requireContext(), getString(), getResources(), parentFragmentManager throw. isAdded is a point-in-time check on only one dimension: it is true while the fragment is on the back stack with no view, which still leaves binding null.
  6. Fix: short term, viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope-based loading, so the request is cancelled when the view dies; long term, load in the ViewModel and render state:
// ViewModel owns the work; survives rotation; cancelled with viewModelScope
val fare: StateFlow<FareUiState> = repo.fareFlow(rideId)
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), FareUiState.Loading)

// Fragment renders only while the view exists and is STARTED
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.fare.collect { binding.fare.text = it.format(resources) }
    }
}

For callback APIs, wrap them with callbackFlow / suspendCancellableCoroutine and awaitClose { call.cancel() } so cancellation reaches the network layer. 7. Prevention: Architecture rule: Fragments hold no async callbacks; they collect state. Lint (detekt custom rule) banning Call.enqueue { ... fragment-method } in Fragments, and requireContext() in lambdas that can outlive the view. Add "pop mid-request" scenario to the regression suite using MockWebServer with a 3 s delay; add Crashlytics keys for lifecycle state. Review action: dashboards for top fragment-related exception signatures per release. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrap everything in try/catch IllegalStateException (swallows real bugs); not use GlobalScope; not cache a reference to the Activity to "avoid requireContext" (leak). A rule of thumb is acceptable: reading strings via applicationContext where no theme is needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• isAdded is true and the view is gone: how? → Fragment is on the back stack; onDestroyView ran but onDetach has not; use viewLifecycleOwner state / view != null for view access.
  • Does the ViewModel approach hit the same crash? → No fragment APIs are touched in the ViewModel, and StateFlow collection is lifecycle-scoped.
  • What about activity?.runOnUiThread { } patterns? → They capture a possibly stale Activity and post even after the Fragment is gone; replace with lifecycle-scoped collection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rewrite from callbacks to state-collecting removed an entire family of crash signatures (about 1% of sessions) without touching a single isAdded check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sprinkles isAdded/try-catch.
  • Hire: ties work to viewLifecycleOwner and explains why isAdded is insufficient.
  • Strong hire: moves work to ViewModel, handles cancellation propagation to the network layer, defines prevention rules and the regression test.

questions.contextHtml: A social app's home screen has a ViewPager2 with 5 tabs (Feed, Reels, Explore, Notifications, Profile) as Fragments; offscreenPageLimit = 4 was set last year "to avoid reload flicker". After the Reels tab launched (video thumbnails) the numbers are: cold-start-to-first-content p95 2.9 s on mid-range phones (target 2.0 s), 11.2% of sessions on 2-3 GB devices use more than 380 MB PSS, OOM crash rate 0.7% on those devices, and every tab fires its first network call in onViewCreated (5 parallel requests, 3 of which are not visible). A Perfetto trace shows 5 fragments inflating layouts in the first 700 ms on the main thread. Red herring: engineers suspect the image library.
questions.promptHtml: How do you reduce startup time and memory without bringing back "flicker" when users switch tabs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the network calls faster / reduce image sizes." Ignores that four invisible tabs do full work at startup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tabs matter at launch (analytics: 82% of sessions land on Feed and stay)? Is "flicker" a visible loading state, or a real data reload? How fresh must tab data be (stale-while-revalidate acceptable)? Which devices matter for the target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set offscreenPageLimit back to the default; defer the data load of non-current tabs; ship as a quick experiment behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Five tab views inflated and five loads started at once: main-thread inflate plus network contention; (b) each tab's RecyclerView pool and bitmaps resident (memory); (c) all tabs RESUMED? (no, non-current are capped at STARTED, but STARTED-scoped collectors run in all of them); (d) image library settings (a smaller factor).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto/System Trace for inflate slices and onViewCreated timing per tab; Android Studio heap dump or dumpsys meminfo per scenario with limit 4 vs default; Network Profiler for parallel requests; a macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric before and after.
  5. Root cause: offscreenPageLimit = 4 forces creation of all five fragments (view inflation and onViewCreated) up front, and STARTED-scoped collectors in non-visible tabs begin work. Memory use is the sum of five view trees plus caches (e.g. 5 x ~40 MB image and view memory = 200 MB if equally heavy; measure, not guess).
  6. Fix:
    • Default offscreenPageLimit, so only visible tabs plus adjacent ones during swipes are alive.
    • Tab data lives in a ViewModel scoped to the host (requireParentFragment() / Activity) with a cache (memory + disk) so recreating a tab view renders instantly (stale-while-revalidate): no flicker without keeping views alive.
    • Start loading in onResume of the current page (the lifecycle contract of ViewPager2), or via a "selected tab" state in the host ViewModel.
    • Use repeatOnLifecycle(RESUMED) for polling-style collectors so background tabs stop.
    • Lazy inflate heavy sub-views (ViewStub), reduce overdraw; RecycledViewPool shared between tabs with the same item type.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI with budgets (startup p50/p95, memory), an alert on PSS p90 per device class, review rule: "ViewPager2 offscreen limit changes need numbers".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keep all fragments alive with hide/show (memory pinned); not delete the cache to save memory (flicker returns); accept a short skeleton placeholder when switching to a tab that has not been visited, instead of paying five tabs' cost on every cold start. Target outcome with numbers: cold start p95 2.9 s -> about 2.1 s (remove four inflations and three parallel calls), PSS p90 380 -> ~260 MB (verify by benchmark).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product insists that Reels must be prefetched → Prefetch data, not the view: warm the repository cache after first content is shown (idle handler / low priority dispatcher).
  • Switching to Reels still stutters on first swipe → Pre-inflate off the critical path via AsyncLayoutInflater is limited; reduce layout complexity and share view pools instead.
  • Does FragmentStateAdapter with offscreenPageLimit = 1 change the lifecycle signals? → Neighbouring pages are created and STARTED; the current one is RESUMED, so keep "visible" work in onResume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A media app cut its cold-start p95 by 600 ms simply by reverting a five-tab offscreen limit, and handled "flicker" with cached state in a shared ViewModel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes image sizes only.
  • Hire: spots offscreen limit and onViewCreated loads, moves loads to onResume.
  • Strong hire: separates view lifetime from data lifetime, measures with Perfetto/macrobenchmark, provides numbers and budgets.

questions.subtopic: Migrating to Navigation under live traffic
questions.contextHtml: A banking app (6M MAU, 40 screens) has a multi-Activity-plus-fragment architecture with hand-written FragmentTransactions (about 140 call sites to replace/add/addToBackStack), several commitAllowingStateLoss() calls, and a custom back stack helper. Leadership wants the Navigation component (Navigation 2.7+) with a single-Activity per feature, with no downtime and no big-bang. Constraints: two release trains per month, crash-free target 99.7%, deep links from SMS and push must keep working, and 30% of users are on Android 9-11 with 3 GB RAM or less. The team has 6 engineers.
questions.promptHtml: How would you plan and execute this migration safely? What are the risks and how do you measure them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite all screens to Navigation in one release and test it." High-risk, unmeasurable, and ignores deep links and back stack semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which flows are highest risk (payments, onboarding)? Are there Activities with launchMode/task flags relied upon? What do analytics and deep link matrix look like? Is multi-module present (graph per feature)? Do we have a back-stack test suite?
  2. Immediate mitigation (stabilize first): Before migrating, remove state-loss crashes in the hand-rolled transactions (guard with lifecycle), because the migration will move them rather than fix them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) Back stack behaviour differences (replace semantics, popUpTo rules, singleTop-like behaviour); (b) deep link breakage and task stack differences; (c) ViewModel scoping changes (nav-graph scopes versus Activity scope) causing stale or lost state; (d) state saved/process death regressions; (e) double navigation on rapid taps ("navigation action cannot be found from current destination", IllegalArgumentException).
  4. How I'd verify each: Characterization tests (record current back behavior in instrumentation tests per flow), deep link matrix test with adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d <uri>, process-death tests (am kill), a staged rollout with Crashlytics cohort comparison, and navigation analytics events.
  5. Root cause (what makes it risky): The old code encodes navigation semantics implicitly in transactions and Activity flags; Navigation encodes them in graph XML with different defaults. Moving 140 call sites risks silent behaviour changes more than visible crashes.
  6. Fix (the plan):
    • Phase 0: baseline metrics, tests, lint to ban new manual transactions.
    • Phase 1: introduce NavHostFragment in one low-risk feature (Settings) in a feature-flagged Activity; host remains legacy in the rest. Keep deep link entry points mapping to old destinations.
    • Phase 2: migrate flow by flow, one graph per feature (nested graph, shared navGraphViewModels scope per flow), behind remote flags to roll back without a release.
    • Phase 3: unify into a single Activity once most flows are on Navigation; retire the custom helper and commitAllowingStateLoss.
    • Navigation entry from legacy code through a small Navigator interface so both worlds coexist:
interface Navigator { fun openBeneficiary(id: String) }
class NavNavigator(private val nav: NavController) : Navigator {
    override fun openBeneficiary(id: String) =
        nav.navigate(BeneficiaryGraphDirections.actionToDetail(id))
}
class LegacyNavigator(private val fm: FragmentManager) : Navigator { /* old transaction */
    override fun openBeneficiary(id: String) { /* ... */ }
}
  1. Prevention: Navigation integration tests with TestNavHostController; a lint rule to forbid FragmentTransaction in new code; ownership of the deep link table with a test per URI; track "time on wrong screen"/back-stack depth analytics; set setReorderingAllowed through Navigation by default.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang rewrite; not mixing two nav hosts inside a single flow; not migrating payments first. Accept temporary dual-stack complexity for 2-3 releases. Navigation hosts fragments via FragmentNavigator (replace-based, views destroyed when stacked), so screens that relied on hide/show to keep view state need ViewModel-backed state first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Crash rate rises 0.1% during Phase 2 → Roll back through the flag for that flow, check cohort signature, add a characterization test, retry.
  • A flow needs two back stacks (bottom tabs) → Use multiple back stacks with NavigationUI state saving (saveState/restoreState in nav 2.4+); verify per flow on low-end devices.
  • Compose adoption coming → Navigation-compose is separate (A4); keeping graph and Navigator boundaries now eases that.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team that migrated one flow per release over five months kept crash-free above target; a peer team that tried a single-release rewrite rolled back after a deep link regression locked users into a loop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite, no metrics.
  • Hire: incremental, flagged, deep link and back stack testing.
  • Strong hire: characterization tests, coexistence interface, ViewModel scope plan, cohort metrics, explicit rollbacks, and risk ordering.

questions.contextHtml: In an e-commerce app, CartFragment shows a Snackbar "Item added to cart" and navigates to Checkout on Events from the ViewModel. The ViewModel exposes LiveData<CartEvent>. Bugs from QA and production (about 3% of sessions touching the cart): (1) after returning from Checkout via back, the Snackbar shows again; (2) after rotating, "Navigate to checkout" fires again and the user is thrown back to Checkout; (3) when the app is in the background and the event arrives, the Snackbar is lost. The team proposes a SingleLiveEvent hack and a Channel with receiveAsFlow(). Red herring: some say it's a Fragment bug and want to avoid the ViewModel.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why each symptom occurs and recommend a design, with trade-offs among SingleLiveEvent, Channel, SharedFlow, and state-based UI.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use SingleLiveEvent" (it handles one observer, drops events with multiple observers or while no observer is active, and hides the problem), or "wrap in Event with a handled flag" without addressing the lost-events case.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "show Snackbar" important enough that losing it (while backgrounded) is a defect, or acceptable? Must navigation happen exactly once even across process death? Are there multiple collectors? Can the UI be modelled as state (e.g. cart count + lastAdded)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mark events as consumed (Event.getContentIfNotHandled()) for the Snackbar and navigation to stop the repeat; add a test for each of the three symptoms.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why they happen): (1) LiveData is state-like: it replays the last value to every new observer; the fragment returns from back stack, onViewCreated observes again with viewLifecycleOwner, and the last event is replayed. (2) Rotation recreates the Activity/Fragment; ViewModel survives; replay again. (3) Channel/SharedFlow without replay drop or lose events when no collector is active (unless buffered).
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit tests with a fake collector lifecycle (TestLifecycleOwner); manual: rotate, back from Checkout, background and foreground; log collector counts.
  5. Root cause: Using a state container (LiveData/StateFlow) to model events. Events are not state: they should be consumed once, but the container's contract is "latest value for new observers".
  6. Fix (recommendation): Prefer modelling as state and have the UI acknowledge consumption (the pattern recommended in Android's architecture guidance for UI events):
data class CartUiState(val items: List<CartItem>, val userMessage: String? = null, val navigateToCheckout: Boolean = false)

class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CartUiState(emptyList()))
    val state: StateFlow<CartUiState> = _state
    fun onAdded() = _state.update { it.copy(userMessage = "Item added to cart") }
    fun messageShown() = _state.update { it.copy(userMessage = null) }
    fun checkoutHandled() = _state.update { it.copy(navigateToCheckout = false) }
}

// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect { s ->
            s.userMessage?.let { Snackbar.make(requireView(), it, LENGTH_SHORT).show(); vm.messageShown() }
            if (s.navigateToCheckout) { findNavController().navigate(R.id.to_checkout); vm.checkoutHandled() }
        }
    }
}

Event stays pending while stopped, is rendered when STARTED, and is cleared after consumption, so no loss and no replay. Channel(BUFFERED) with receiveAsFlow() delivers each event once, buffers while no collector (limited to capacity), but is fan-out (single consumer), drops on overflow, and is lost on process death; it is a reasonable choice for pure "fire-and-forget" things like haptics. SharedFlow(replay = 0) loses events when nobody collects. SingleLiveEvent is deprecated practice (single observer, warns on multiple observers). 7. Prevention: Architecture guidelines doc: "events are state with an ack"; tests simulate lifecycle (stop, recreate); lint/detekt flags SingleLiveEvent and MutableSharedFlow used for UI events without justification. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: State+ack adds boilerplate and requires idempotent ack handling (double consumption if two collectors); mitigate with a single collector in the view lifecycle. I would not use the Event wrapper long-term: it is a hidden mutable flag in an immutable state. I would not use GlobalScope or the Activity as an event bus.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the pending event survive process death? → Navigation intent, usually not; keep it in memory only. If it must (e.g. a pending purchase confirmation), store a durable state in SavedStateHandle or persistence.
  • Two collectors (Fragment and a dialog) consume the same flag → Only the owner screen collects it; dialogs request via the Result API.
  • Testing → Use runTest, collect with TestScope, assert messageShown() clears the field.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promotions banner re-appeared after every back navigation for a year because it was posted through LiveData; switching to a state-and-ack model removed the bug and the "viewed twice" analytics inflation of about 8%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: recommends SingleLiveEvent without understanding replay.
  • Hire: explains LiveData replay and uses an event wrapper or Channel correctly.
  • Strong hire: argues state-with-ack, enumerates lifecycle edge cases (stopped, recreated, process death) and trade-offs of Channel vs SharedFlow, with tests.
